newsitem.title: GERMANY: German MP warns against watering down tax reform.
newsitem.headline: German MP warns against watering down tax reform.

text.p: Gunnar Uldall, leading tax reform parliamentarian of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), warned on Wednesday against watering down the tax reform proposal the party adopted last week.
The CDU passed a resolution that Germany should cut its top income tax rate to 35 percent from the current 53 percent.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, under pressure to bring Germany's budget deficit into line to qualify for the single European currency in 1999, told the CDU party congress Bonn faces tough choices to cut spending to finance tax rate cuts.

Uldall said at a book presentation he accepts the CDU plan even though it is less radical than his own, which would have cut the top rate to 28 percent, financed by eliminating virtually all deductions.
Tax policy makers must now avoid a spiral of concessions, reinstating various deductions that would nudge tax rates back up, making the plan unacceptable to anyone, Uldall said.
"The work of the interest groups and lobbyists has already begun," Uldall said. "The mice have begun to nibble, to make sure they get their own little piece of the big pie."
Former finance minister Gerhard Stoltenberg said the planned tax reform could mean a net 20 billion mark reduction in Germans' tax burden.
A tax reform commission headed by Finance Minister Theo Waigel is due to forge a proposal by the end of the year, for implementation by 1999.
Kohl has said the value-added tax would have to be raised to offset at least part of any cut in income taxes, which critics fear would eliminate the hoped-for stimulative impact on the economy.
The German Federation of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT) on Wednesday endorsed the CDU tax reform plan, which would also sharply reduce government subsidies.
